summary: The output of a design team analyzing different IPv6 link models for IEEE 802.16 networks. It examines considerations for each model and where each fits under different deployment scenarios. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A team compared different ways to wire a wireless network for IPv6 and wrote down which works best in which situation.

questions: how to connect ipv6 to wireless networks
subtitle: Three ways to connect IPv6 devices to wireless networks

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.16 wireless networks need to run IPv6, but the technology lacks native multicast at the link layer, leaving multiple deployment options.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes three link models: shared IPv6 prefix (all devices share one prefix), point-to-point (each device gets its own prefix), and Ethernet-like (emulates a shared broadcast link via bridging).
tldr.outcome: The Ethernet-like model was chosen for Ethernet Convergence Sublayer deployments, while the point-to-point model is recommended for IP Convergence Sublayer with IPv6 classifiers due to its simplicity.

today: RFC 4968 is an Informational document that provided analysis to guide IPv6 deployment in WiMAX networks during their development. The point-to-point model became the standard approach for IP Convergence Sublayer implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IEEE 802.16 is a point-to-multipoint wireless technology for last-mile broadband access, often called WiMAX. The standard defines downlink multicast support but not uplink multicast, creating challenges for running standard IPv6 protocols that assume bidirectional multicast at the link layer.

This document examines how to run IPv6 over 802.16 networks by analyzing three different link models. Each model makes different trade-offs between complexity, address space efficiency, and compatibility with existing IPv6 behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless networks send data one way to many devices easily but struggle with devices sending to many others. IPv6 normally expects this two-way ability, so this document figures out how to work around that.

sections.title: The Three Link Models
sections.content:
The RFC presents three fundamental approaches to mapping IPv6 onto 802.16 wireless networks.

Shared IPv6 Prefix Link Model: All mobile stations attached to an access router share one or more IPv6 prefixes. Devices construct their own global addresses from this shared pool. The link between each mobile station and the access router is point-to-point at Layer 2, but at the IPv6 layer, all devices appear on the same link. This model requires special handling of duplicate address detection using MLD snooping and relay mechanisms at the access router.

Point-to-Point Link Model: Each mobile station receives a unique, separate prefix from the access router. The link between each station and the router acts as a standard IPv6 point-to-point link. This allows standard IPv6 address autoconfiguration and duplicate address detection to work unchanged. It is the simplest model from a protocol perspective.

Ethernet-Like Link Model: The access network is configured to emulate a shared Ethernet broadcast link through bridging between base stations and the access router. This allows standard Ethernet and IPv6 behaviors to work as designed, including native multicast support and standard address autoconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: Model 1 is like a classroom where all students share the same seat range numbers but sit apart. Model 2 gives each student their own unique seat number. Model 3 pretends it's all one big table so everyone can talk to everyone at once.

sections.title: Key Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The shared prefix model does not require protocol changes but needs implementation changes at the access router for relay duplicate address detection. It cannot support direct inter-device sharing of services because devices on a shared public network should not expose personal resources.

The point-to-point model reuses existing RFC specifications (RFC 2461, 2462) unchanged and presents full consistency with standard IPv6 link definitions. However, it prevents shared link-local services, making it unsuitable for enterprise networks where devices discover and use shared printers or other services on the local segment.

The Ethernet-like model preserves all IPv6 standards and can emulate multicast through unicast forwarding with MLD snooping. Its primary drawback is implementation complexity, requiring bridging between base stations and the access router.

All models handle renumbering identically: the access router must withdraw old prefixes and advertise new ones. The point-to-point model requires sending renewal advertisements individually to each mobile station, while the other models can send one advertisement that reaches all stations through the base station.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared model works but needs special tricks at the router. The point-to-point model is simplest but breaks office sharing. The Ethernet model is complex but works like regular networks. Changing addresses affects all of them the same way.

sections.title: Dormant Mode and Routing
sections.content:
Mobile stations in dormant mode reduce power consumption by listening only on a paging channel. The network pages the mobile station when packets arrive, and the station transitions to active mode to receive them.

Multicast capability can cause unnecessary wake-ups. The shared prefix and point-to-point models avoid this: the shared model has no multicast, and the point-to-point model has only one other node on the link. The Ethernet-like model requires multicast filtering at the base station to prevent waking devices for multicast groups they have not joined.

Routing protocols must account for the link model chosen. The shared prefix model at the MAC level is point-to-point between each mobile station and base station, then extended via tunnel to the access router. The point-to-point link model presents intentionally limited provider-edge connectivity. Other models may impact routing protocol behavior significantly.
sections.plainLanguage: Sleeping phones wake up when needed. Multicasting (one message to many) could wake too many devices by accident, especially in the Ethernet model. Different models affect how routers learn about the network.

sections.title: Conclusions and Recommendations
sections.content:
For deployments using Ethernet Convergence Sublayer, the Ethernet-like link model is the only option proposed and is consistent with how IPv6 runs over Ethernet.

For IP Convergence Sublayer with IPv6 classifiers, the point-to-point link model is recommended as the primary choice. It offers simplicity in duplicate address detection, requires no new protocols, and does not break existing IPv6 applications. The shared IPv6 prefix model is defined as an alternative if service provider communities express interest in shared link-local services.

The design team concluded that the point-to-point model best balances protocol compatibility, implementation simplicity, and applicability to typical service provider (cellular network) deployments where shared link services are not required.
sections.plainLanguage: If using wired-like technology, fake a wired network. If using IP style, give each phone its own addresses because it's the simplest and works with all existing software.
